items.title: Three Powers of Disturbance: Intoxication, Madness, Dreaming

items.zh: 云何醉？謂由依止性羸劣故，或不習飲故，或極數飲故，或過量飲故，便致醉亂。
items.en: What is intoxication? It is because the support [the mind relies on] has grown weak; or because one is unaccustomed to drinking; or because one drinks too often; or because one drinks too much — through any of these, intoxication and confusion result.

items.zh: 云何狂？謂由先業所引，或由諸界錯亂，或由驚怖失志，或由打觸末摩，或由鬼魅所著，而發癲狂。
items.en: What is madness? It is brought on by past karma; or by disorder among the bodily elements; or by losing one's composure through terror; or by a blow to a vital point of the body; or by being possessed by a spirit — through any of these, derangement arises.

items.zh: 云何夢？謂由依止性羸劣；或由疲倦過失；或由食所沈重；或由於闇相作意思惟；或由休息一切事業；或由串習睡眠；或由他所引發，如由搖扇，或由明呪，或由於藥，或由威神；而發惛夢。
items.en: What is dreaming? It is because the support has grown weak; or through the fault of exhaustion; or because one is weighed down by food; or through dwelling in attention on the mark of darkness; or from resting from all activity; or through habituated sleep; or through being induced by another — as by the waving of a fan, by an incantation, by medicine, or by another's spiritual power — through any of these, dim dreaming arises.

items.zh: 云何覺？謂睡增者不勝疲極故，有所作者要期睡故，或他所引，從夢而覺。
items.en: What is waking? It is when one whose sleep has grown can no longer bear the exhaustion; or when one who has something to do has set the hour to rise beforehand; or when induced by another — through any of these, one wakes from dream.

items.zh: 云何悶？謂由風熱亂故；或由捶打故；或由瀉故，如過量轉痢及出血；或由極勤勞；而致悶絕。
items.en: What is fainting? It is through disturbance of wind and heat; or through being struck; or through excessive purging, as in severe diarrhea or blood loss; or through extreme exertion — through any of these, fainting results.

items.zh: 云何醒？謂於悶已而復出離。
items.en: What is reviving? It is emerging again from a faint.

items.zh: 云何發起身業、語業？謂由發身語業智前行故；次欲生故；次功用起故；次隨順功用為先，身語業風轉故；從此發起身業、語業。
items.en: What is the initiating of bodily and verbal action? It is: first, the deliberating cognition that precedes bodily and verbal action arises; next, the intention arises; next, the exertion arises; and next, following on that exertion, the "wind" [that drives] bodily and verbal action turns — and from this, bodily and verbal action is initiated.

items.zh: 云何離欲？謂隨順離欲根成就故，從他獲得隨順教誨故，遠離彼障故，方便正修無倒思惟故，方能離欲。
items.en: What is freedom from desire? It comes about through the ripening of roots conducive to freedom from desire; through receiving fitting instruction from another; through being free of the obstacles to it; and through skilfully cultivating undistorted reflection — through these, freedom from desire becomes possible.

items.title: Falling Back from Freedom of Desire

items.zh: 云何離欲退？謂性軟根故；新修善品者，數數思惟彼形狀相故；受行順退法故；煩惱所障故；惡友所攝故；從離欲退。
items.en: What is falling back from freedom of desire? It is: because one's faculties are dull by nature; because one newly cultivating wholesome practice dwells again and again on the marks of former conduct; because one takes up a state conducive to falling back; because one is obstructed by afflictions; or because one falls under the sway of bad companions — through any of these, one falls back from freedom of desire.

items.zh: 云何斷善根？謂利根者，成就上品諸惡意樂現行法故；得隨順彼惡友故；彼邪見纏極重圓滿到究竟故；彼於一切惡現行中，得無畏故；無哀愍故；能斷善根。
items.en: What is cutting off wholesome roots? It is: because one of sharp faculties gives rise to superior degrees of evil intent, made an ongoing activity; because one falls in with bad companions who reinforce this; because one's wrong views become utterly thorough and fixed; because one grows fearless in the midst of every kind of unwholesome activity; and because one is without compassion — through these, wholesome roots are cut off.

items.zh: 此中種子亦名善根，無貪瞋等亦名善根。但由安立現行善根相違相續，名斷善根；非由永拔彼種子故。
items.en: Here, both the seed and the active presence of non-greed, non-hatred, and the like are called wholesome roots. But it is only by establishing an unbroken opposition to their active presence that one is said to cut off wholesome roots — not by permanently uprooting the seed itself.

items.zh: 云何續善根？謂由性利根故；見親朋友修福業故；詣善丈夫聞正法故；因生猶豫，證決定故；還續善根。
items.en: What is renewing wholesome roots? It is: because one's faculties are sharp by nature; because one sees close friends engaged in meritorious action; because one goes to a good person and hears the true teaching; or because doubt has arisen and is then resolved into certainty — through these, wholesome roots are renewed.

items.title: Death: Three Causes, Two Kinds, Three States of Mind

items.zh: 云何死？謂由壽量極故，而便致死。此復三種。謂壽盡故，福盡故，不避不平等故。當知亦是時非時死。或由善心，或不善心，或無記心。
items.en: What is death? It is that death results because one's life-span is exhausted. This, again, is of three kinds: death from the exhaustion of one's life-span, death from the exhaustion of one's merit, and death from failing to avoid what is out of balance. These should also be understood as timely death and untimely death. And it may come with a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind.

items.zh: 云何壽盡故死？猶如有一，隨感壽量滿盡故死，此名時死。云何福盡故死？猶如有一，資具闕故死。
items.en: What is death from the exhaustion of one's life-span? It is when someone dies simply because the life-span apportioned to them by past karma has run its full course — this is called timely death. What is death from the exhaustion of merit? It is when someone dies because the requisites of life have become lacking, their merit having been used up.

items.zh: 云何不避不平等故死？如世尊說：九因九緣，未盡壽量而死。何等為九？謂食無度量，食所不宜，不消復食，生而不吐，熟而持之，不近醫藥，不知於己若損若益，非時、非量行非梵行，
items.en: What is death from failing to avoid what is out of balance? As the Blessed One said: there are nine causes and nine conditions by which one dies before one's life-span is exhausted. What are the nine? Eating without moderation; eating what does not agree with one; eating again before what was already eaten has been digested; not expelling what should be expelled; letting what has already ripened into illness take hold unchecked; not resorting to physicians and medicine; not knowing what benefits or harms oneself; and engaging in sexual misconduct at an improper time, or to an improper degree.

items.zh: 此名非時死。
items.en: This is called untimely death.

items.title: The Three States of Mind at Death

items.zh: 云何善心死？猶如有一，將命終時，自憶先時所習善法；或復由他令彼憶念。由此因緣，爾時信等善法現行於心，乃至麁想現行。若細想行時，善心即捨，唯住無記心。所以者何？彼於爾時，於曾習善亦不能憶，他亦不能令彼憶念。
items.en: What is dying with a wholesome mind? It is when someone, as they are about to die, recalls the wholesome practises they cultivated before — or is helped to recall them by another. Through this, faith and the other wholesome qualities become active in the mind, so long as thought remains at the coarse level. Once thought turns subtle, the wholesome mind is relinquished, and only an indeterminate mind remains. Why is this? Because at that point one can no longer recall what one once practised as wholesome, nor can another bring it to mind for one.

items.zh: 云何不善心死？猶如有一，命將欲終，自憶先時串習惡法；或復由他令彼憶念。彼於爾時，貪瞋等俱諸不善法現行於心，乃至麁、細等想現行，如前善說。
items.en: What is dying with an unwholesome mind? It is when someone, as death approaches, recalls the unwholesome deeds they were long habituated to — or is reminded of them by another. At that time, craving, hatred, and other unwholesome states become active in the mind. The same progression from coarse to subtle thought applies here as in the wholesome case.

items.zh: 又善心死時，安樂而死；將欲終時，無極苦受逼迫於身。惡心死時，苦惱而死；將命終時，極重苦受逼迫於身。又善心死者，見不亂色相。不善心死者，見亂色相。
items.en: Moreover, one who dies with a wholesome mind dies at ease: as death approaches, no extreme painful feeling presses upon the body. One who dies with an unwholesome mind dies in distress: as death approaches, extreme painful feeling presses upon the body. Further, one who dies with a wholesome mind perceives unconfused forms; one who dies with an unwholesome mind perceives confused forms.

items.zh: 云何無記心死？謂行善不善者，或不行者，將命終時，自不能憶，無他令憶。爾時非善心非不善心死。既非安樂死，亦非苦惱死。
items.en: What is dying with an indeterminate mind? It is when one who has done wholesome or unwholesome deeds, or neither, is at the point of death unable to recall them, with no one else able to bring them to mind either. At that time, one dies with neither a wholesome nor an unwholesome mind — neither at ease, nor in distress.

items.zh: 又行善不善補特伽羅，將命終時，或自然憶先所習善及與不善，或他令憶。彼於爾時，於多曾習力最強者，其心偏記，餘悉皆忘。
items.en: Further, when a person who has done good or bad deeds is about to die, they either recall of their own accord the good or bad they practised before, or are reminded of it by others. At that time, of the many things they have practised, the mind holds especially to whichever is strongest, and forgets all the rest.

blocks.text: We continue through the seventeen powers that only the mental consciousness has. Today's passage moves quickly through altered states (intoxication, madness, dreaming, waking, fainting, reviving), then the initiating of action, then four powers concerning the spiritual life (becoming free of desire, falling back, cutting off and renewing wholesome roots), and finally death. Each power is defined by its causes, so the reading is a series of short lists.

Two short passages are missing from Ru-Yi's translation, and we have supplied our own: at 0281b14, the sentence "this is called untimely death", which closes the list of nine causes; and at 0281c03–c05, what the dying mind holds on to.

subs.head: Altered states belong to the mental consciousness

blocks.text: Why are drunkenness, madness, and dreaming called "powers" of the mental consciousness? Because the five senses cannot be drunk or deranged; only the mind that thinks and judges can lose its balance. Note the variety of causes: some are physical (a weakened body, a blow to a vital point, 末摩, *marman*), some emotional (terror), some karmic, some from outside (a spirit, a drug, an incantation).

Venerable Miào Jìng defines dreaming as a state in which "the five senses are inactive while the sixth consciousness is active". Master Cháng Bǎi adds that only beings of the desire realm dream; beings of the form and formless realms do not sleep, and so do not dream.

Chinese uses two different words here. 覺 is coming out of sleep; 醒 is coming out of a faint. Venerable Miào Jìng points out what fainting shows: the sixth consciousness stops, yet one can revive, because the ālayavijñāna is still present in the body. When the ālayavijñāna leaves, that is death. We will meet this point again in the account of dying.

The treatise gives four steps before any bodily or verbal act: first a deliberating cognition, then intention, then exertion, then the "wind" that moves the body and voice. Venerable Miào Jìng matches the first three with the three kinds of **volition** (思, *cetanā*): deliberative volition (審慮思), decisive volition (決定思), and impelling volition (動發思). The "wind" is the breath and bodily energy.

Two teaching points follow. Master Cháng Bǎi: nothing we say or do is really sudden; it only seems so because the first steps pass too quickly to notice. Venerable Miào Jìng: we often say that mental karma *is* greed, hatred, and delusion, "but it is not. It is the volition that acts together with greed, hatred, and delusion. It is the commander-in-chief." This is why Yogācāra locates karma in volition.

subs.head: Freedom from desire, and falling back

blocks.text: **Freedom from desire** (離欲, *vairāgya*) here means freedom from sensual desire through meditative attainment. It needs four things: ripened roots, fitting instruction, freedom from obstacles, and skilful cultivation of right reflection. Venerable Miào Jìng warns that instruction alone "is only accepting it intellectually"; desire is actually left behind only through cultivation.

One can fall back. Among the causes, Master Cháng Bǎi singles out "taking up a state conducive to falling back": enjoying the joy, ease, or reputation that comes with an attainment instead of pressing on. Advertising an attainment invites the admiration that undoes it.

The **wholesome roots** (善根, *kuśala-mūla*) are non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Strikingly, the first cause of cutting them off is *sharp* faculties turned to evil. Venerable Miào Jìng: "A person of sharp faculties is especially keen, especially intelligent; but if it veers a little, the result is dreadful."

Then comes one of the most hopeful sentences in the fascicle. What is cut off is only the *active presence* of the wholesome roots; their seeds are never destroyed. Venerable Miào Jìng: "Cutting off wholesome roots cuts off their active presence, not the seed." Master Cháng Bǎi draws the conclusion: no one is permanently unable to change. This is the seed theory of Day 1 put to work.

Wholesome roots are renewed through sharp faculties, the example of friends, hearing the true teaching, or doubt that is resolved into certainty. Venerable Miào Jìng links the last cause to the five minds of Day 2: doubt is the seeking mind, and certainty is the deciding mind.

Death is classified two ways. By cause, there is death because one's life-span is exhausted (timely death), because one's merit is exhausted, or because one failed to avoid what is out of balance (both untimely). The nine causes of untimely death are mostly about diet and health; the *Pīxún jì* explains that "nine causes and nine conditions" are the same nine things seen from two angles, not eighteen.

subs.head: Dying with a wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate mind

blocks.text: By state of mind, death may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The key distinction is between coarse and subtle thought. While thought is still **coarse** (麁想, clear and focused), a dying person can recall good deeds or be reminded of them, and faith and other wholesome states become active. Once thought turns **subtle** (細想, dim and unfocused), the wholesome mind falls away and only an indeterminate mind remains.

Venerable Miào Jìng draws a very practical lesson from "helped to recall them by another": keep a written record of the good you have done, item by item, and ask a good friend to read it to you at the end, while you can still hear. Master Cháng Bǎi adds a caution against hasty judgement: physical pain at death is not, by itself, proof of an unwholesome life.

The sentence at 0281c03 (our translation) completes the picture: at death the mind fastens on whatever was practised most often and most strongly. What we do repeatedly now is what we will remember then.

quiz.q: According to Venerable Miào Jìng, how do "waking" (覺) and "reviving" (醒) differ?
options: they mean the same thing
waking belongs to the mental consciousness, reviving to the eye-consciousness
coming out of sleep is called 覺; emerging from a faint is called 醒
waking is by day, reviving by night
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Coming out of sleep is called 覺. Coming out of a faint is called 醒." The text itself says, "What is reviving? It is emerging again from a faint." He adds that in fainting and in dreamless sleep the sixth consciousness is at rest; one can revive from a faint because the ālayavijñāna is still present — when it departs, that is death. The translation renders the two as "waking" and "reviving," and English-speaking students should note how the two Chinese characters divide the work.

quiz.q: The treatise sets out the sequence by which bodily and verbal action is initiated. Which order is correct?
options: the "wind" turns → exertion arises → intention arises → deliberating cognition comes first
first the deliberating cognition that precedes action arises → next intention → next exertion → next the "wind" that drives bodily and verbal action turns
intention → deliberating cognition → the "wind" turns → exertion
exertion → intention → deliberating cognition → the "wind" turns
quiz.why: "First, the deliberating cognition that precedes bodily and verbal action arises; next, the intention arises; next, the exertion arises; and next, following on that exertion, the 'wind' [that drives] bodily and verbal action turns — and from this, bodily and verbal action is initiated." Venerable Miào Jìng maps these onto three volitions: the deliberating cognition is deliberative volition, intention is decisive volition, exertion is impelling volition (the *Pixunji* agrees); the "wind" is the in- and out-breath pervading the body. Master Cháng Bǎi notes that nothing we say or do is ever really sudden — it only looks that way because the first three steps pass too quickly to notice.

quiz.q: According to Venerable Miào Jìng, how do those who fall back from freedom of desire and those who cut off wholesome roots contrast in their faculties?
options: those who fall back have "soft," dull faculties; those who cut off wholesome roots, surprisingly, have sharp faculties — great intelligence, but turned a little astray, with dreadful results
both have dull faculties
both have sharp faculties
those who fall back have sharp faculties, those who cut off roots dull ones
quiz.why: The text gives "faculties dull by nature" as the first cause of falling back, but says cutting off wholesome roots happens "because one of sharp faculties gives rise to superior degrees of evil intent." Venerable Miào Jìng: "A person of sharp faculties is especially keen, especially intelligent — but if it veers a little, the result is dreadful." This runs against the intuition that only the dull fall. Master Cháng Bǎi adds that the very sharpness that can cut off wholesome roots can also renew them (§30, "because one's faculties are sharp by nature").

quiz.q: When the treatise speaks of "cutting off wholesome roots," what exactly is cut off?
options: the seed of the wholesome roots, permanently uprooted
the ālayavijñāna
the eye and the other faculties
only an unbroken opposition to the active presence of wholesome roots is established — the seed itself is not permanently uprooted
quiz.why: "But it is only by establishing an unbroken opposition to their active presence that one is said to cut off wholesome roots — not by permanently uprooting the seed itself." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Cutting off wholesome roots cuts off their active presence, not the seed." Master Cháng Bǎi treats this as the whole point of the passage: because the seed survives, "no one is permanently unable to change; even the worst person can be rescued." A is exactly what the text denies.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the three kinds of death?
options: dying with a wholesome, an unwholesome, or an indeterminate mind
death from the exhaustion of one's life-span, death from the exhaustion of one's merit, and death from failing to avoid what is out of balance
composed death, uncomposed death, and sudden death
death in the desire, form, and formless realms
quiz.why: "This, again, is of three kinds: death from the exhaustion of one's life-span, death from the exhaustion of one's merit, and death from failing to avoid what is out of balance. These should also be understood as timely death and untimely death." A is the other classification given in the same passage (by the state of mind at death) and is the closest trap; C comes from §35. Master Cháng Bǎi's lecture: exhaustion of life-span is timely death; exhaustion of merit and failing to avoid imbalance are untimely deaths.

quiz.q: For one dying with a wholesome mind, what happens once thought turns subtle?
options: the wholesome mind grows stronger
it turns into an unwholesome mind
the wholesome mind is relinquished, and only an indeterminate mind remains; one can no longer recall what one practised as wholesome, nor can another bring it to mind
one immediately sees the intermediate being
quiz.why: "Once thought turns subtle, the wholesome mind is relinquished, and only an indeterminate mind remains. … At that point one can no longer recall what one once practised as wholesome, nor can another bring it to mind for one." The *Pixunji*: thought that images clearly and sharply is coarse; thought that drifts dim and unfocused is subtle. Hence a dying person should be helped to recall good deeds while thought is still coarse. Master Cháng Bǎi adds a caution: physical suffering at death is not, by itself, proof of an unwholesome life.
